Ehh, but the only non-scarcity angle I see for bitcoin is the introduction of new alt coins (e.g. ether, zcash, ripple). That's kind of like saying gold/silver aren't scarce because there are other elements, and we could create/discover new materials in the lab. But the new materials don't have intrinsic value until they find a useful role, particularly one that isn't better served by an existing material, and further that doesn't necessarily remove value from existing materials so much as create new value (depending on the specifics of introducing a new capability vs. improving on an existing one.)

The article shows a great example, of the fellow buying stuff internationally via bitcoin trade for amazon credit. Yeah gold works for local and in-person trade, but that loses a lot of value to overhead if you want to buy something far away and have to rely on secure shipping, and those remote goods are particularly valuable specifically because they aren't available locally.

Trading gold for amazon credit fundamentally means shipping physical goods out of Venezuela in return for the credit, whereas trading bitcoin fundamentally means exchanging one form of credit (amazon) for another credit (proof of work on the network, aka mining) and can be done entirely on the internet, relatively anonymously. In a failed state, it will be much less practical for them to ship trade goods out of the country (both for politics as well as needing those goods themselves), than to trade credits based on running computer services (which is like doing a job, creating new value in the world).

It's important to remember Bitcoin isn't fiat, it represents work done running the network itself (validating transactions), and has a functional use in transmitting that credit with low overhead, and with a degree of privacy, all without the risk of government inflation. Many of these values are shared by precious metals, but the metals lack the long-distance liquidity.

Diversification is important, I wouldn't bet 100% on cryptocurrency myself, I'm just arguing it has a valid role in the portfolio.

The closest to what you are suggesting is a fork like Litecoin or Bitcoin Cash. However, if you follow the numbers when this happens, it isn't inflationary because people get their holdings cloned on both chains following the fork. So in a sense yes new coins were created, but they were also assigned to the people who already held the original coin, so holders don't lose any total value, i.e. the total valuation of the two coins remains consistent (sometimes it increases as apparently people are more confident in the future of each coin policy individually than endless deadlock of arguing between the two policies on a single coin.)

Other coins are completely new code bases with very different algorithms for how they are mined and used. For example Ethereum is focused on providing a form of financial cloud computing, able to autonomously execute contracts to trigger transactions, and in a secure and decentralized way. So if you think "all of the other new coins" come from forking, you have embarrassingly little idea what you are talking about.
